name: Adam Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a powder-coating spray booth, hanging metal brackets and checking the first pieces after they leave the oven. I came from a garden centre that closed, so I am a junior still learning this machine at fifty-eight with secondary schooling. My pay is about typical for an operator, and I like a clean even edge.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and what tools do you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Fran works in a home-goods shop, and our grown children have their own households. We rent, have about five months of expenses saved and a few similar plants nearby. I use an AI phone app now and then to summarise safety notices, after a colleague showed it worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the powder-coating crew that a little AI help with shift notes is fine. The first bracket still needs a person to look for a bare corner after it leaves the oven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I came from a closed garden centre and am still learning the spray booth at fifty-eight. Fran works at a home-goods shop, our children are grown, and five months saved helps us cover the rent if one wage is briefly late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep hanging metal brackets, checking first parts and using the same AI phone app now and then to summarise safety notices. From each full paid month I would add fresh money to our reserve after rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm about the job. I know the booth is new to me, but the senior operator checks my first batch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you spot a bad coating?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bare corner on a coated bracket stays dull where powder did not reach it. I ask the senior operator before changing the gun pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did you start using AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A colleague showed me the notice summary last spring after it worked for him. I read the actual safety sheet before touching the booth.

say: I would accept **small note savings** from AI.
I would still inspect **first coated brackets** for bare corners.
think: Our **five-month reserve** can cover a short late wage.
I still need **senior checks** while learning the spray booth.
do: Keep **spray-booth shifts** and inspect first brackets.
Use the **existing AI app** for safety-note summaries.
Save fresh **full-month wages** after rent and food.
feel: **Calm** about work with a useful cash buffer.
S0.quote: A bare corner on a coated bracket stays dull where powder did not reach it.
fieldNote: Adam is **junior at fifty-eight** after a late change from garden-centre work.
His **five-month reserve** and Fran’s shop income support calm, while extra saving comes from new paid wages.

steps.text: Keep coating shifts and inspect first brackets
Save fresh full-month surplus after rent and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor to show how AI ordering affects shifts before anyone promises faster coating. A robot hanger may arrive more slowly, and it needs a guarded test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The camera could judge the simple bare corners I spot now, and a robot might load the hooks. I am still the junior operator, so my paid week could shrink; Fran’s shop wage alone would not cover our rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request the next two rosters and watch a colleague run the camera. If the plant offers a paid guarded practice place with a qualified setter, I would learn its new AI reject controls on test brackets; after actual hours fall, I would apply for posted reachable coating or packing jobs only where net pay after travel covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about my own shifts, but I can test the new screen if it is offered safely. A screen that flags a blemish still needs someone to find the bad gun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would supervise the practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The setter would isolate the conveyor and let me change a reject threshold on test parts. Watching from behind the line would not teach me the control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would another plant be reachable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are a few, but I would check their posted shifts and bus fare. I would not move to a job that pays less after travel.

say: I would seek **written shift rosters** before robot hanging changes the powder-coating crew.
I would ask for a **guarded camera trial**.
think: My **junior checking hours** could be reduced by a camera.
Fran’s **shop wage** cannot meet our rent alone.
do: Request **two rosters** and watch a proven camera run.
Learn **new AI reject controls** only if offered paid guarded practice.
Apply after **hour cuts** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay coating work.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible cut to his own paid week.

fieldNote: His **steady style** starts with a colleague’s proven camera before new instruction.
Practice needs an **offered paid safe place**; another job needs a posting, workable shifts and net wages after travel.

steps.text: Request two rosters and observe proven camera use

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AGI may arrive by 2028 when I am sixty, while capable hands-on robots reach coating around 2031 when I am sixty-three. Planning changes first; hook loading comes later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most junior hanging and inspection hours to go when robots can do both. Five months saved and Fran’s shop wage will not cover rent through a long loss of my pay; I would lie awake calculating the months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel the planned family trip and ask for written staffing dates. If my paid shifts end, I would apply only for posted reachable factory work at net pay after travel covering our bills; if no adequate job appears, I would ask the landlord about temporary terms and a local employment adviser about posted openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by a large likely wage loss. I can make calls, but I cannot turn a closed vacancy into a pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children pay rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households. I would ask one for a ride to an interview if the timing fits, not put their wages in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need actual pension and household figures before that decision. We have no guarantee that five months saved will bridge to enough income.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 coating robots.
I would ask for **written staffing dates** before a cut.
think: I expect **junior hanging hours** to disappear with capable robots.
Five **months saved** and one shop wage cannot carry long rent costs.
do: Cancel **family trip** and request staffing dates.
Apply after **lost shifts** only for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work.
Ask **landlord and adviser** for possible help if no adequate job appears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless rent sums.
S2.quote: I can make calls, but I cannot turn a closed vacancy into a pay slip.
fieldNote: His **age sixty-three** at physical robot arrival does not guarantee retirement income.
Job and support routes require **real conditions**: lost shifts, a posted reachable vacancy, net pay after travel and landlord agreement.

steps.text: Cancel family trip and request written staffing dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the plant that thinking AGI in 2031 arrives when I am sixty-three and capable coating robots around 2034 when I am sixty-six. Five years is enough to learn a safer maintenance task if someone offers paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can spot a poor spray edge now, but I cannot repair the booth. I would consider a recognised spray-equipment certificate only if a local plant needs it at a wage that covers our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my coating shift and add fresh surplus from full paid months to savings. If the employer offers a funded booth-maintenance course on paid time with an actual isolated practical place and a posted reachable maintenance job at bill-covering net pay, I would enrol; after qualifying, I would apply for that role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, but five years lets me check a real vacancy before class begins. I do not want to hold a certificate while the rent waits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe practice look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fitter would isolate the spray gun and let me replace a worn nozzle before a test run. I would need an offered paid supervised slot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no course place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid shifts and check posted local operator jobs if hours begin to fall. I would not spend our reserve on an unfunded evening class.

say: I would ask for **paid practical learning** before 2034 robots.
I would seek a **posted maintenance wage** before enrolling.
think: My **rent** still needs a regular paid wage when I reach sixty-six.
A **spray certificate** only helps if local work exists.
do: Keep **coating shifts** and save fresh full-month surplus.
Enrol in **funded paid booth training** only with offered safe place and adequate posted job.
Apply after **qualification** for that reachable maintenance role.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to compare a real offer.
S3.quote: I do not want to hold a certificate while the rent waits.
fieldNote: His **current coating skill** could bridge into maintenance only through real practical teaching.
The later application needs **offered safe training**, a posted reachable role and bill-covering net wages.

steps.text: Save fresh full-month surplus while keeping coating shifts
Enrol if funded paid safe booth place and adequate posted job exist
Apply after qualification for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay maintenance job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight and capable coating robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. A decade is time to check the work and retirement numbers, not a reason to guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children will have their own lives, and Fran’s shop hours may change. Five months saved today is a useful buffer, but I cannot say a future pension will cover our rent and repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the coating shift and put fresh full-month surplus into savings after bills. I would request retirement figures with Fran; in the first year after 2036, if still employed because we need wages, I would compare real rosters and apply after sustained cuts only for safe reachable work with bill-covering net pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about the distant robots while our current income is steady. A figure on a statement only helps when it covers the actual bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if pension income and Fran’s confirmed pay cover rent, food and a repair buffer. If they do not, I would keep safe paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn another control at sixty-eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I still work and receive an offered paid safe place, I would try it after seeing someone else succeed. I cannot promise a vacancy then.

I would keep **2036 AGI** separate from 2039 coating robots.
think: Our **rent and repair costs** will still matter even if the robots arrive late.
A future **pension amount** may not replace wages.
do: Keep **2026 coating shifts** and save fresh surplus after bills.

feel: **Uneasy** about distant robots while current income stays steady.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable coating robots around 2031 could remove junior shifts when I am sixty-three. Written staffing dates, funded paid safe training and posted reachable jobs at bill-covering net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the first bracket after the oven. I want the person using a gate or hand test to be paid for doing it carefully.

headlineQuote: I want the person using a gate or hand test to be paid for doing it carefully.
portrait: **Adam**, 58, is a junior powder-coating operator after a late move from garden-centre work, with secondary schooling and developing machine skill.
His **shop-worker partner**, grown children, rent, typical pay, five-month reserve and some local plants give a limited buffer.
He uses **AI occasionally** for safety notices and learns new camera controls only through offered paid guarded practice.
Fast robots threaten **coating hours** at sixty-three; longer warning supports conditional maintenance training and retirement-income review.
biggestWorry: **Fast physical robots** could remove junior coating shifts around 2031 before his household can afford to stop working.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered funded safe instruction and posted reachable work at bill-covering net pay would help.
